fuller.text: This report asks whether today's AI systems, or ones built soon, could be conscious. It was written by a team of neuroscientists, philosophers and AI researchers. Their approach is to take the best-supported brain-science theories of consciousness and check whether AI systems work in the ways those theories describe.

sentences.text: This report asks whether today's AI systems, or ones built soon, could be conscious.
It was written by a team of neuroscientists, philosophers and AI researchers.
Their approach is to take the best-supported brain-science theories of consciousness and check whether AI systems work in the ways those theories describe.

fuller.text: The authors say the question is becoming pressing. AI is improving very fast, and leading researchers borrow ideas linked to consciousness in human brains to make AI more capable. Meanwhile, chatbots that convincingly imitate human conversation will likely lead many people to believe these systems are conscious. The authors take seriously that conscious AI could be built within the next few decades, which raises deep moral and social questions.

fuller.text: By "conscious" the authors mean having subjective experience: there is "something it is like" to be the system. Seeing a screen, hearing birdsong or feeling an itch are examples. By contrast, much clever processing in the brain, such as controlling hormone release, happens with no experience at all.

fuller.text: The method rests on three assumptions. First is computational functionalism: running the right kind of computation is both needed and enough for consciousness, whatever the system is made of. The authors adopt this as a working assumption, not a proven fact, and so leave out integrated information theory, which rejects it. Second, scientific theories of consciousness have real evidence behind them. Third, a "theory-heavy" approach is best, judging how a system works inside rather than how it behaves, since AI can be trained to mimic human talk.

The authors adopt this as a working assumption, not a proven fact, and so leave out integrated information theory, which rejects it.
Second, scientific theories of consciousness have real evidence behind them.
Third, a "theory-heavy" approach is best, judging how a system works inside rather than how it behaves, since AI can be trained to mimic human talk.

fuller.text: From the theories, the authors draw 14 "indicator properties": features that make a system more likely to be conscious if it has them. Recurrent processing theory asks for perception in which information loops back, applying the same step repeatedly, and builds organised pictures of a scene. Global workspace theory asks for many specialised parts sharing a small "workspace" whose contents are broadcast to all of them. Higher-order theories ask for a system that monitors its own perceptions, judging which are reliable and which are just noise. Attention schema theory asks for a model of the system's own attention, and predictive processing asks for perception built on constantly predicting incoming input. Agency means learning from feedback to pursue goals, and embodiment means modelling how one's own actions change what one senses.

fuller.text: The authors find that most indicators could be built with standard machine-learning methods, though combining several would take experimenting. Some are already common, such as information looping back in many networks. Reinforcement learning, where a system learns by trial and reward, is arguably enough for the basic form of agency.

fuller.text: They then test real systems. For large language models built on the Transformer design, they find only a weak case for any workspace indicator, partly because information never loops back. The Perceiver, a design with a small shared space, comes closer but lacks broadcast to all parts. Of three agents in robot or virtual bodies, DeepMind's AdA may be the likeliest to count as embodied by their standards.

fuller.text: The authors name limits. The indicators need interpreting, and making them sharper would go beyond what the theories claim. Knowing a system's design and training is not always enough; one may need to inspect what it has learned internally. And meeting the indicators would not mean a system is definitely conscious.

fuller.text: Their conclusion is that no current AI system is a strong candidate for consciousness. Yet they see no obvious technical barriers to building systems that meet the indicators. If computational functionalism is true, conscious AI could realistically be built in the near term. They warn that both missing real consciousness and wrongly seeing it carry risks, and call for more research.

brief.text: This report asks whether today's AI systems could be conscious, meaning able to have experiences. It matters because AI is improving fast, and chatbots that talk like people may lead many to believe they are conscious.

brief.text: The authors draw on brain science theories of how consciousness works. From them they build a checklist of "indicator properties", features that make a system more likely to be conscious. They conclude no current AI looks conscious, but nothing obvious stops AI from being built with these features.
